title: Thermal curtains and blinds as window insulation
subtitle: How lined curtains and cellular blinds reduce window heat loss overnight
excerpt: A single-glazed window with no window covering loses heat constantly. Closing a heavy lined curtain against the frame adds a still-air layer that roughly halves the effective U-value through the combined assembly. Cellular or honeycomb blinds work similarly for windows where curtains are impractical. Neither is a substitute for double glazing, but both make a measurable overnight difference.
sourceNotes: CIBSE Guide A window thermal performance data. Energy Saving Trust window and curtain guidance. British Standards BS EN 13363 for solar protection devices.

glossaryTerms.definition: A measure of how fast heat passes through a building element. Expressed in W/m2K. A single-glazed window is around 5.7; the window-plus-closed-curtain assembly drops to roughly 2.8 at night.

content.text: Windows are the largest single thermal weakness in most homes. A 1.5 m2 single-glazed window loses around 20 kWh per month through the glass alone in a UK winter. Closing a heavy lined curtain over the same window drops the combined

from 5.7 to roughly 2.5 to 3.0 W/m2K, similar in performance to basic double glazing, for as long as the curtain is closed. The catch is that a curtain only works thermally if it seals at the sides, bottom, and top. A curtain that hangs free from the wall lets cold air convect behind it, defeating the insulating effect.
Three conditions must be met for a curtain to provide useful thermal insulation:
The curtain must have a thermal lining, a separate lining fabric with a layer of bonded batting or interlining. Standard curtain lining fabric provides almost no thermal benefit.

The curtain track or pelmet must sit close to the wall or ceiling, not set well away from it. A gap of more than 100 mm between track and window allows convective cooling of the air behind the curtain.
The curtain must extend at least 50 mm onto the sill or floor at the bottom and overlap the wall by at least 150 mm on each side beyond the window frame.

Cellular (honeycomb) blinds use a double-wall structure of air cells to resist heat flow. A top-down, bottom-up cellular blind mounted inside a double-glazed window frame reduces the unit's overall U-value by 0.5 to 0.9 W/m2K when closed. For a window that already has double glazing, the cellular blind reduces the effective U-value from 1.6 to around 0.8 to 1.1. These figures come from manufacturer certified test data; specific performance depends on blind depth, cell size, and how well the blind seals at the edges.

Thermal curtains and blinds only reduce heat loss when they are closed. During the day, a south-facing window with a closed curtain blocks solar gain that could warm the room passively. In winter, the net thermal gain from passive solar heating through a south or south-west window can exceed the overnight conductive heat loss. The correct operating pattern is: open south-facing curtains whenever the sky is clear and the sun is above the horizon; close all curtains at dusk.

A 1960s bungalow in Sheffield has 20 m2 of single-glazed windows. Current overnight heat loss through the glass: 20 m2 × 5.7 W/m2K × 10°C temperature difference = 1,140 W continuously for 12 hours overnight = 13.7 kWh per night. With thermal-lined curtains properly fitted (effective U-value 2.8 for the assembly): 20 m2 × 2.8 × 10 = 560 W × 12 hours = 6.7 kWh. Saving: 7 kWh per night, around 1,200 kWh per heating season, roughly 1,200 kWh per heating season. The thermal lining pays back in under 2 years.
